status: Ten scoped proposed regional connections; map finding aid only

associations.name: Eno
associations.associationType: Historical river-community geography in state and specialist accounts
associations.period: Early European-contact history; state management plan dated September 2017
associations.sourceTitle: Eno River State Park General Management Plan — North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation
associations.evidenceNote: The state plan identifies Eno people living along the Eno River at early European contact. Jean B. Anderson's Library of North Carolina account independently locates the historical Eno in North Carolina's Piedmont. This supports a historical North Carolina connection without assigning a modern Eno government or adopting uncertain descendant-identification claims.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual PDF cover, mission text and printed page 3 (PDF page 2), II. HISTORY, especially lines 31–34 identifying Eno, Shakori and Occoneechee along the river. Supporting Anderson, Eno Indians (2006), first geographic paragraph was read in complete indexed article text; direct NCpedia fetch returned 403. No old profile source was reused.
limits: Historical state connection only. Related Siouan peoples and contemporary descendant governments are not interchangeable.
No archaeological site coordinates or exclusive territorial outline are reproduced.

associations.name: Erie
associations.associationType: Historical lakeshore settlement described by county government
associations.period: Historical settlement before the mid-seventeenth century; undated county account
associations.sourceTitle: History of Erie County — Erie County, Pennsylvania
associations.evidenceNote: Erie County's own history identifies the Eriez people as the source of the Pennsylvania county's name and describes their settlement on its lakeshore. This is a specific Pennsylvania historical connection for the Erie access point, rather than an inference from a modern lake or city name. Inspection limit: indexed original-source text was inspected; the direct page could not be rendered in this review. This is an inspected excerpt, not a full-work content check.
associations.reviewedScope: The county's indexed opening paragraph and explicit page identification as Erie County, PA were read. Direct fetch timed out. The paragraph actually names Eriez people; it is not a modern canal or unrelated Erie County source. The account's claim that the people were destroyed is not adopted.
limits: Indexed primary text inspection is disclosed; direct page content could not be independently retrieved in this bounded pass.
The connection makes no extinction claim, identifies no present representative government and does not mark the entire Erie homeland.

associations.name: Flathead (Bitterroot Salish)
associations.associationType: Specific constituent people within a present confederated government
associations.period: Continuing confederated community connection; public account inspected October 21, 2026
associations.sourceTitle: Who We Are — Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes
associations.evidenceNote: CSKT identifies Bitterroot Salish as one of its three distinct constituent nations, discusses their Montana reservation connection, and publishes its Pablo, Montana government address. Its explanation says Flathead is associated with the reservation name and favors the peoples' specific identities. The directory's older Flathead access label therefore points here without treating all CSKT peoples as Bitterroot Salish.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML History & Culture paragraph at line 496; explanation of CSKT and Flathead at line 541; tribal mailing-address block. The companion Séliš-Ql̓ispé Culture Committee page was also inspected, but its restricted archives were not accessed.
limits: Bitterroot Salish, Upper Pend d'Oreille and Kootenai are distinct constituent nations.
Only Montana is proposed; the combined territorial description is not indiscriminately assigned to each constituent nation.

associations.name: Guale
associations.associationType: Documented historical community and mission-era connection
associations.sourceTitle: St. Catherines Island, GA — National Park Service
associations.evidenceNote: NPS explicitly describes Guale people living on St. Catherines Island in Georgia's Sea Islands during the mission era. This provides a Georgia historical-community connection; the former Spanish Florida jurisdiction does not turn the record into a present-day Florida location.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML Quick Facts location, and opening history paragraph at line 46 identifying both Guale people and Georgia's Sea Islands. Additional mission-era paragraphs were read only to establish historical context.
limits: No public-access invitation is implied: the source identifies the island as private and not open to the public.
No mission site coordinates, territorial polygon or contemporary community identity claim is reproduced.

associations.name: Hatteras
associations.associationType: Historical people-name and coastal geography in specialist reference
associations.period: Sixteenth- through eighteenth-century historical naming; essay published 2006
associations.sourceTitle: Croatoan Indians — Phillip W. Evans, Encyclopedia of North Carolina / NCpedia
associations.sourceType: Specialist historical encyclopedia essay hosted by the Library of North Carolina
associations.evidenceNote: Evans explicitly identifies Croatoan/Croatan as a group later known as Hatteras Indians and locates their historical communities on North Carolina's Outer Banks. The proposed connection concerns that historical people-name usage, without deciding the present representation or recognition of communities using Roanoke-Hatteras or related names. Inspection limit: indexed original-source text was inspected; the direct page could not be rendered in this review. This is an inspected excerpt, not a full-work content check.
associations.reviewedScope: Complete indexed 2006 essay read, especially the first paragraph's explicit Hatteras alias, island geography and later reference to coastal North Carolina. No inaccessible NPS report or uninspected Dare County resolution is relied on. The essay's statement that no tribal entities survive is excluded.
limits: Indexed text inspection, not a claimed successful direct fetch, is disclosed.
The 2006 essay is not a current recognition-status or descendant-community assessment.
Specific village, archaeological and burial locations are omitted.

associations.name: Hitchiti
associations.associationType: Historical regional geography in specialist scholarship
associations.period: Early-contact historical geography described in a regional essay
associations.evidenceNote: The essay identifies Hitchiti among the native inhabitants of southern Georgia's wiregrass region and places them along the Ocmulgee River. This supports a Georgia historical connection for the people-name access point; it does not locate a particular Hitchiti tribal town or equate every Hitchiti-speaking town with that town.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML Human History paragraph at line 98 explicitly naming Hitchiti and wiregrass Georgia. Only the geographic identification is used; the essay's qualified de Soto-era dating is not converted into a definite settlement date.
limits: Hitchiti can designate a town and a broader language/people context; the limited regional source does not resolve every use.
No contemporary government, complete territorial range or settlement coordinates are asserted.

associations.name: Kalaallit
associations.associationType: Contemporary people-name and country identification in specialist reporting
associations.sourceTitle: The Indigenous World 2026: Kalaallit Nunaat (Greenland) — IWGIA
associations.evidenceNote: IWGIA's country introduction explicitly states that most Greenlandic Inuit refer to themselves as Kalaallit and places this identification in Kalaallit Nunaat, Greenland. This supports Greenland as one connection while preserving the report's distinction among regional names and communities. It does not equate all people residing in Greenland with Kalaallit. Inspection limit: indexed original-source text was inspected; the direct page could not be rendered in this review. This is an inspected excerpt, not a full-work content check.
associations.reviewedScope: Full indexed country-introduction text inspected, including the explicit Kalaallit self-identification sentence and following regional-group distinctions. The direct open returned an empty rendering. Demographic percentages, legal characterizations and political/current-affairs claims are not adopted.
limits: Indexed original-report text, not a successful direct rendering, supplies the inspected passage.
Kalaallit is a broader access label with regional naming differences; no distinct-nation count or exclusive identity boundary is implied.

associations.name: Karankawa
associations.associationType: Traditional coastal homeland in specialist scholarship
associations.period: Traditional and early-contact homeland described in the revised reference essay
associations.sourceTitle: Karankawa Indians — Carol A. Lipscomb, revised by Tim Seiter, Handbook of Texas
associations.evidenceNote: The essay explicitly locates traditional Karankawa homelands on Texas's Gulf Coast and explains that the name encompasses several coastal groups. Only the broad Texas connection is indexed; the account does not justify collapsing the groups into a single historical government.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML opening geographic and naming paragraph at line 9 and author/reviser credits at lines 6–8. Later passages were not used for this limited map finding aid.
limits: No precise homeland boundary, cultural-practice description or current descendant/recognition-status claim is adopted.
The source's later accounts of violence and ceremonial practices are outside the scope of this connection.

associations.name: Kaska
associations.associationType: Named constituent First Nations and communities in a provincial record
associations.period: Provincial listing updated April 15, 2024; inspected October 21, 2026
associations.sourceTitle: Kaska Nation — Province of British Columbia
associations.evidenceNote: The Province explicitly identifies Kaska communities in British Columbia, including Dease River, Kwadacha and Lower Post, alongside Yukon connections. British Columbia is proposed as one useful connection for the broader Kaska entry, without implying that Kaska people or governments are confined to that province.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML Current activities paragraph at line 44, the listing's date and Information/Members section. No linked agreement is claimed as read and no count of distinct governments is inferred from overlapping cross-border listings.
limits: Kaska is a broader people-name access point, not an interchangeable name for one council or one First Nation.
The listing is dated; current negotiations, population figures and exact territorial boundaries are outside this finding aid.

associations.name: Kathlamet
associations.associationType: Ancestral constituent-people geography in the Nation's self-description
associations.period: Ancestral-community identification described in the Nation's public account
associations.sourceTitle: The Chinook Indian Nation — Who We Are
associations.evidenceNote: The Nation explicitly identifies Cathlamet (Kathlamet) as a constituent people of present-day Oregon. This directly supplies the spelling relationship and an Oregon connection, while preserving the distinction between a constituent people and the shared Chinook Indian Nation government. Inspection limit: indexed original-source text was inspected; the direct page could not be rendered in this review. This is an inspected excerpt, not a full-work content check.
associations.reviewedScope: Complete indexed Who We Are text inspected, especially the first constituent-list paragraph naming Cathlamet (Kathlamet) and Oregon. The same wording was independently present in the indexed July 22, 2021 Chinook vs. Chinookan article. Direct community-site opens timed out; no treaty text or legal-status review is claimed.
limits: One historical state connection is proposed, not a denial of Kathlamet connections on both sides of the Columbia River.
The constituent description does not make all Chinookan peoples citizens of one government or adjudicate present recognition status.

batchLimits: Only the ten assigned access points were reviewed; no canonical profiles, map data or Site files were edited.
Seven focused web batches were used. Failed and redirected sources were not repeatedly retried.

Erie, Hatteras, Kalaallit and Kathlamet rely on explicitly disclosed indexed source passages because direct rendering failed, timed out or was unavailable. Their published geography is clear, but independent direct-render checks remain useful.
Map connections are finding aids. They do not supply exhaustive homelands, population counts, rights boundaries or a review of contemporary recognition.
Eno and Erie were verified from fresh relevant sources rather than the unrelated source cards previously attached to those profile stubs.
